w: A Gato-class submarine, the first US Navy ship named for the croaker, a fish that makes drumming and throbbing noises underwater. Commissioned during the Second World War, she now sits preserved as a museum ship on the Buffalo waterfront, her torpedo tubes and cramped berths open for walk-throughs.
s: Named for a fish that drums and throbs underwater
_facts: first US Navy ship named for the croaker fish
preserved museum ship on the Buffalo waterfront

w: Founded in 1875, this is the seventh-oldest zoo in the United States, tucked into 23.5 acres of Delaware Park alongside more than 320 plant species. It pulls roughly 400,000 visitors a year, ranking as Western New York's second-biggest tourist draw after Niagara Falls itself, and stays open year-round.
s: America's 7th-oldest zoo, second only to Niagara Falls
_facts: 23.5 acres in Delaware Park, 320+ plant species
~400,000 visitors a year, 2nd biggest WNY draw

w: Built in 1901 for the Pan-American Exposition -- the same fair where McKinley was shot a few blocks away -- this Beaux-Arts hall by architect George Cary is one of the few structures from that fair still standing, now a National Historic Landmark holding the city's historical society collection.
s: A surviving hall from the 1901 Pan-American Expo
_facts: houses the Buffalo Historical Society collection

w: This 1912 Beaux-Arts skyscraper reprised a temporary tower from Buffalo's 1901 Pan-American Exposition, its terra-cotta cladding etched with electricity motifs now seen as a precursor to Art Deco. Its spire still turns gold and blue for Sabres playoff runs and crowns the city's own New Year's ball drop.
s: A deco precursor crowned by Buffalo's own ball drop
_facts: based on a temporary tower from the 1901 Expo
electricity motifs seen as an Art Deco precursor
hosts the annual Buffalo Ball Drop

w: Seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Buffalo since its founding in 1847, this cathedral stands at 50 Franklin Street inside downtown's Joseph Ellicott Historic District -- the mother church for a diocese that today stretches across eight counties of Western New York.
s: Mother church for an eight-county diocese
_facts: within the Joseph Ellicott Historic District

n: Buffalo and Erie County Botanical Gardens
w: Frederick Law Olmsted laid out the grounds and Lord & Burnham built the Victorian glasshouses -- a three-way collaboration with botanist and plant-explorer John F. Cowell, all folded into Olmsted's own South Park on Buffalo's south side.
s: Olmsted's park, Victorian glass, a plant-hunter's eye

w: In 1907 the Vatican proclaimed this East Side parish the first basilica in the United States, a rare honor for a Polish immigrant congregation. Built in the deliberately opulent Polish Cathedral style, it still displays the original proclamation, in Latin and its English translation, inside its own museum room.
s: The first basilica ever proclaimed in the US
_facts: serves a Polish immigrant East Side parish
displays the original proclamation in a museum room

w: Formerly the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, this modern and contemporary art museum sits opposite Buffalo State University and the Burchfield Penney Art Center in Delaware Park. Its new name stitches together donors from different eras: Gilded Age industrialist John Albright, and hedge-fund manager Jeffrey Gundlach.
s: Three donors, a century apart, one renamed museum
_facts: adjacent to Delaware Park, opposite Buffalo State University
named for donors John Albright, Seymour Knox II, Jeffrey Gundlach

w: Commissioned in mid-1945, too late for WWII combat, this cruiser was rebuilt into a guided-missile flagship, her forward guns stripped for the Talos missile system. She served as Sixth Fleet flagship in the Mediterranean before 1976 -- the last surviving Cleveland-class cruiser, now moored in Buffalo.
s: The last surviving Cleveland-class cruiser afloat
_facts: converted to a Talos guided-missile cruiser

w: A 96-foot obelisk in Niagara Square, standing at the exact point where all of Buffalo's main roads converge. Raised in 1907 to William McKinley, shot in the city during the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, its obelisk form was urged by planner Daniel Burnham himself as the shape best suited to the monument's gravity.
s: The obelisk where all of Buffalo's roads converge
_facts: marks the center where Buffalo's main roads meet

w: This national shrine in neighboring Lackawanna grew out of the charitable works of Father Nelson Baker, whose social-welfare projects still draw pilgrims to the site year-round. Part of the Diocese of Buffalo, it stands as one of the country's few basilicas built on the strength of one priest's fundraising.
s: A basilica built on one priest's charity work
_facts: founded through Father Nelson Baker's charities
part of the Diocese of Buffalo

w: Designed by the father-and-son team of Eliel and Eero Saarinen, this Symphony Circle hall has hosted the Buffalo Philharmonic since it was built and still hosts the Buffalo Chamber Music Society besides. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1989 for its architecture, 49 years after it first opened.
s: A Saarinen father-son design, still the Philharmonic's home
_facts: designed by Eliel and Eero Saarinen
home of the Buffalo Philharmonic Orchestra
also hosts the Buffalo Chamber Music Society

n: Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site
w: Inside the Ansley Wilcox House on Delaware Avenue, Theodore Roosevelt took the presidential oath on September 14, 1901, hours after William McKinley died of wounds from an assassination at the city's Pan-American Exposition -- the only US presidential inauguration ever held in Buffalo.
s: Where Teddy Roosevelt took the oath after McKinley died
_facts: followed McKinley's assassination at the Pan-American Expo
only US inauguration held in Buffalo

w: Frank Lloyd Wright's first commercial commission, built in 1906 for the Larkin Soap Company's sprawling mail-order operation. Abandoned after the company folded in the 1940s, it sat derelict for years before being demolished in 1950, its remains used as landfill. The Seneca Street site is now simply a parking lot.
s: Frank Lloyd Wright's first office building, now a lot
_facts: Frank Lloyd Wright's first commercial design
built 1906 for the Larkin Soap Company
left derelict after the company's lease ended
demolished 1950, site now a parking lot
